title: From microwaves to megamasers
caption: Galaxies MCG+01-38-004 and MCG+01-38-005, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: MCG+01-38-004, MCG+01-38-005 · constellation Virgo · about 400 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Two galaxies appear in this Hubble image, one above the other. The upper, red-tinted one is MCG+01-38-004. The lower, blue-tinted one is MCG+01-38-005, and it hides an unusual power source at its heart.

The lower galaxy has an active galactic nucleus, an especially bright and intense center thought to be driven by a supermassive black hole that drags in surrounding material and throws out jets and radiation. That energy pours into nearby clouds of water. The hydrogen and oxygen atoms in the water absorb some of it and give it back at particular wavelengths, one of them in the microwave range. That makes MCG+01-38-005 a water megamaser, a far stronger cousin of the microwave lasers called masers.
Objects like this are useful tools. Astronomers used its microwave emission to refine the Hubble constant, which describes how fast the Universe is expanding.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.49 x 1.46 arcminutes) and distance (400 million light years), the frame spans roughly 290,000 × 170,000 light-years. Its light set out about 400 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image was taken with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 in near-ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared filters. The color assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: The microwave glow that makes the lower galaxy special does not appear in this picture. Hubble recorded ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light, some of it beyond what the eye can see.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Microwaves are the same kind of radiation used to heat food. Across the Universe, objects give off light across the whole spectrum, from high-energy gamma rays to low-energy microwaves and radio waves.
The Hubble constant is named after Edwin Hubble, whose observations revealed that the Universe is expanding and after whom the space telescope is named.
alt: Two galaxies, one above the other, the upper one red-tinted and the lower one blue-tinted.
